content: Odontogenic infections are infections that originate within a tooth or the surrounding supporting structures. These infections typically remain localized to the tooth and its immediate area but can sometimes spread to adjacent or distant regions. The term odontogenic is derived from the Greek words odous (tooth) and genos (birth), reflecting the origin of these infections. Odontogenic infections progress through three distinct stages: the inoculation stage, the cellulitis stage, and the abscess stage. It is estimated that 90-95% of all orofacial infections arise from the teeth or their supporting structures, such as in cases of acute periapical periodontitis or periapical abscesses. The second most common type of odontogenic infection is the periodontal abscess. Odontogenic sinusitis refers to inflammation of the paranasal air sinuses caused by infections associated with the teeth. Approximately 20% of maxillary sinusitis cases are attributed to odontogenic origins. This condition is often caused by a periapical or periodontal infection of a maxillary posterior tooth, where inflammatory exudate erodes through the bone superiorly and drains into the maxillary sinus. Once an odontogenic infection involves the maxillary sinus, it has the potential to spread further to the orbit or the ethmoid sinus. Treatment of odontogenic infections typically involves antimicrobial therapy, among other interventions, depending on the severity and extent of the infection.
